5b020000-0000-4000-8000-000000000005.passage: Before the invention of the mechanical clock, many towns in medieval Europe kept time by the ringing of church bells. Church bells helped organize many parts of daily life in medieval European towns.

d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000013.passage: Honeybees communicate the location of food through a "waggle dance." The angle of the dance relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun, while the duration of the waggle portion signals how far away the food is.

5b020000-0000-4000-8000-000000000009.passage: The octopus has a remarkable ability to change color, yet most octopus species appear to be colorblind, possessing only one type of light-sensitive cell in their eyes. octopus skin proteins prevent the animals from changing color.

octopuses sense some information about light through their skin rather than only through their eyes.

5b020000-0000-4000-8000-000000000018.passage: The architect of a new library chose to place its reading rooms along the north side of the building. Light from the north, she explained, is indirect and consistent throughout the day, so ______

the library would need no electric lighting at night.
readers would have steady light without harsh glare or shifting shadows.

5b020000-0000-4000-8000-000000000013.passage: Paleontologists long assumed that a group of large, long-necked dinosaurs browsed on tall trees, like modern giraffes. The dinosaurs' teeth were similar in shape to those of other large plant-eaters.
Modern giraffes have neck vertebrae that allow little side-to-side movement.
5b020000-0000-4000-8000-000000000013.explanation: If the dinosaurs mostly ate low-growing plants, that directly supports the claim that they fed on low vegetation rather than tall trees.

Passage I — Reviving the Lot on Alder Street
For years, the empty lot on Alder Street was __a place that was full and crowded with__ weeds, broken glass, and an abandoned shopping cart. Most neighbors walked past it without a second glance, my aunt Rosa saw something different. She had grown up on a farm, and they imagined rows of tomatoes and beans where the trash now lay.

In the spring of 2019, Rosa organizes a meeting at the community center. Only six people came. Therefore, they left with a plan: they would ask the city for permission to use the lot, and they would clean it themselves.

The cleanup took three weekends. Volunteers hauled away two hundred bags' of trash, tested the soil, and built twelve raised beds out of donated lumber. By the following summer, the garden had a waiting list of families eager for a plot.

Today the garden grow more than vegetables. Children learn where food comes from, older residents trade recipes, and neighbors who once had barely known each other now share tools and advice. Rosa likes to say that the garden's best harvest have been friendship.

5b030000-0002-4000-8000-000000000013.passage:
Passage II — Libraries on Wheels
In the early twentieth century, many rural Americans lived miles from the nearest library. To reach them, some counties began sending libraries out on __wheels__. These "book wagons," later known as bookmobiles, were often converted carriages and, later, trucks lined with sturdy, wooden, shelves.

One of the earliest began operating in Washington County, Maryland, in 1905. A librarian, named Mary Lemist Titcomb thought of and came up with the idea of a horse-drawn wagon that would carry books directly to farms and villages. However, the wagon traveled routes through the countryside, stopping at general stores and farmhouses.

The service was popular, and families who had owned only a few books could suddenly borrow dozens each year. When the original wagon was destroyed in an accident, the county eventually replace it with a motorized truck.

Passage III — The Long Notes
I was eleven when I first picked up a cello. It was my __mothers'__, a dented instrument she had played in her high school orchestra, and it smelled faintly of rosin and old wood. My first attempts sounded like a door creaking open in a horror movie.

My teacher, Mr. Okafor, wouldn't never allow me to rush. For the first month, he had me play nothing but long notes that were slow and also long in their duration on open strings. Therefore, I wanted to play real music, not exercises, and I told him so. He smiled and said, "The music is in the long notes."

It wasn't until my first recital, two years later, that I understood what he meant. As I played a simple melody, I noticed that every note was steady, and full the the result of all those hours spent on open strings. Looking out at the audience, I felt for the first time that the cello and I were speaking the same language.

I still play every day. Before I practice anything else, I play long, slow notes, just as Mr. Okafor taught me — and each one remind me of my favorite composers.
5b030000-0003-4000-8000-000000000024.prompt: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
5b030000-0003-4000-8000-000000000024.explanation: The cello belongs to one mother, so the singular possessive "mother's" is correct.

Passage IV — Helping the Monarchs
Each fall, millions of monarch butterflies __migrates__ from Canada and the northern United States to the mountains of central Mexico, a journey, of up to 3,000 miles. No single butterfly makes the entire round trip; it takes several generation's for the population to return north.

Fortunately, the eastern monarch population has declined sharply since the 1990s. Scientists point to several different multiple causes, including the loss of milkweed, the only plant on which monarch caterpillars can feed. As farms and suburbs have expanded, milkweed has disappeared from much of the monarchs' range.

Volunteers across the continent are trying to help. Schools plant milkweed gardens, and highway departments let roadside plants grow instead of mowing them. Citizen scientists tag butterflies with small stickers, allowing researchers to track where individual monarchs travel.

5b050000-0001-4000-8000-000000000001.passage:
Passage I — Literary Narrative: This passage is from a short story.

On the last day the shop was open, my grandfather wound every clock in it, though he knew no customer would come to hear them. There were forty-one of them, from the tall walnut case clock by the door to the small brass carriage clocks lined up on the shelf behind the counter, and he went from one to the next with the same unhurried care he had shown them for thirty-eight years.

"They should go out the way they came in," he said when I asked why he bothered. "Running."

I had come to help him pack, but for most of the morning there was little to do except watch. He had sold the building months before, and the new owners planned to open a phone repair store. My mother had told me that Grandpa was relieved to be retiring, that his eyes were no longer good enough for the tiny gears, and that he was looking forward to fishing. But standing in the narrow room, with all the clocks ticking slightly out of step, like a crowd of people talking at once, I wasn't sure she was right.

Around noon a woman came in carrying a shoebox. Inside was a wristwatch with a cracked face. It had been her father's, she said, and it hadn't worked in years. She'd seen the sign in the window and hoped she wasn't too late.

My grandfather looked at the watch for a long moment. Then he cleared a space on the counter, switched on the lamp, and fitted his loupe to his eye. I had seen him do this a thousand times, but I watched now as if for the first time: the way his hands, which shook slightly when he held a coffee cup, became perfectly still over the open watch.

It took him almost an hour. When he finally handed it back, the second hand was sweeping smoothly around the cracked face. The woman tried to pay him, and he waved the money away.

"Last job," he said. "On the house."

After she left, he sat for a while without speaking. Then he stood, took one of the carriage clocks from the shelf, and wrapped it carefully in newspaper.

"For you," he said, placing it in my hands. "You'll have to wind it yourself."

5b050000-0001-4000-8000-000000000001.explanation: The passage centers on the shop's last day — winding the clocks, the final repair, the gift — as observed by the narrator.

There were forty-one of them, from the tall walnut case clock by the door to the small brass carriage clocks lined up on the shelf behind the counter, and he went from one to the next with the same unhurried care he had shown them for thirty-eight years.

"They should go out the way they came in," he said when I asked why he bothered. "Running."

I had come to help him pack, but for most of the morning there was little to do except watch. He had sold the building months before, and the new owners planned to open a phone repair store. My mother had told me that Grandpa was relieved to be retiring, that his eyes were no longer good enough for the tiny gears, and that he was looking forward to fishing. But standing in the narrow room, with all the clocks ticking slightly out of step, like a crowd of people talking at once, I wasn't sure she was right.

Around noon a woman came in carrying a shoebox. Inside was a wristwatch with a cracked face. It had been her father's, she said, and it hadn't worked in years. She'd seen the sign in the window and hoped she wasn't too late.

My grandfather looked at the watch for a long moment. Then he cleared a space on the counter, switched on the lamp, and fitted his loupe to his eye. I had seen him do this a thousand times, but I watched now as if for the first time: the way his hands, which shook slightly when he held a coffee cup, became perfectly still over the open watch.

It took him almost an hour. When he finally handed it back, the second hand was sweeping smoothly around the cracked face. The woman tried to pay him, and he waved the money away.

"Last job," he said. "On the house."

After she left, he sat for a while without speaking. Then he stood, took one of the carriage clocks from the shelf, and wrapped it carefully in newspaper.

"For you," he said, placing it in my hands. "You'll have to wind it yourself."

5b050000-0001-4000-8000-000000000002.explanation: He says, "They should go out the way they came in…Running."

Passage II — Social Science: This passage is adapted from an essay about decision-making.

Most people believe that their important choices reflect their own preferences. When we enroll in a retirement plan, choose a health insurance option, or decide whether to become an organ donor, we assume we have weighed the alternatives and picked the one we want. Research in behavioral economics suggests that the situation is more complicated: very often, the option we end up with is simply the one that was already selected for us.

Economists call this pre-selected option the default. A default is what happens if a person does nothing. For decades, many employers required workers to sign up actively for retirement savings plans; workers who never filled out the form were not enrolled. When some companies reversed this arrangement, automatically enrolling new employees while allowing them to opt out at any time, participation rose dramatically. The workers' options had not changed at all. Only the starting point had.

Why should a starting point matter so much? Researchers point to several forces. Choosing requires effort, and even a few minutes of paperwork can be enough to make people postpone a decision indefinitely. Defaults can also carry an implied endorsement: people may assume that whoever chose the default did so for good reasons. Finally, people tend to feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains, so giving up an option they already "have" can feel like a loss.

Similar patterns appear in other areas. Countries in which citizens are organ donors unless they opt out tend to have far higher registration rates than countries that require people to opt in, even when surveys show that attitudes toward donation are similar.

This power raises difficult questions. If those who design forms and policies inevitably influence choices, there may be no truly neutral way to present options. Some scholars argue that designers should therefore choose defaults that most people would want if they thought carefully, while keeping it easy to choose differently. Critics respond that this approach places too much trust in designers' judgment about what is best for others. Both sides agree on one point, however: the question is not whether defaults shape decisions, but how.

5b050000-0002-4000-8000-000000000010.explanation: The passage argues that defaults often determine outcomes, and it explores why and what that means.

Most people believe that their important choices reflect their own preferences. When we enroll in a retirement plan, choose a health insurance option, or decide whether to become an organ donor, we assume we have weighed the alternatives and picked the one we want. Research in behavioral economics suggests that the situation is more complicated: very often, the option we end up with is simply the one that was already selected for us.

Economists call this pre-selected option the default. A default is what happens if a person does nothing. For decades, many employers required workers to sign up actively for retirement savings plans; workers who never filled out the form were not enrolled. When some companies reversed this arrangement, automatically enrolling new employees while allowing them to opt out at any time, participation rose dramatically. The workers' options had not changed at all. Only the starting point had.

Why should a starting point matter so much? Researchers point to several forces. Choosing requires effort, and even a few minutes of paperwork can be enough to make people postpone a decision indefinitely. Defaults can also carry an implied endorsement: people may assume that whoever chose the default did so for good reasons. Finally, people tend to feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains, so giving up an option they already "have" can feel like a loss.

Similar patterns appear in other areas. Countries in which citizens are organ donors unless they opt out tend to have far higher registration rates than countries that require people to opt in, even when surveys show that attitudes toward donation are similar.

This power raises difficult questions. If those who design forms and policies inevitably influence choices, there may be no truly neutral way to present options. Some scholars argue that designers should therefore choose defaults that most people would want if they thought carefully, while keeping it easy to choose differently. Critics respond that this approach places too much trust in designers' judgment about what is best for others. Both sides agree on one point, however: the question is not whether defaults shape decisions, but how.

choices: the cost of registering as a donor.
the number of hospitals in each country.
how the choice is presented rather than differences in attitudes.
differences in how strongly citizens support donation.
5b050000-0002-4000-8000-000000000015.explanation: The passage notes attitudes are similar even though registration rates differ — pointing to the opt-in/opt-out design.

5b050000-0003-4000-8000-000000000019.passage:
Passage III — Humanities: This passage is adapted from an essay by a literary translator.

People often ask me whether a translation can ever be faithful to its original. The question assumes that faithfulness is a single, simple thing — that a translator's job is to find, for every word in one language, its twin in another. Anyone who has tried to translate even a short poem knows that this is not how languages work.

Consider the problem of a single word. The language I translate from has a word for the particular quiet of a house after guests have left: not silence exactly, but a silence that still holds the shape of conversation. English has no such word. I can explain it in a phrase, as I have just done, but a phrase is heavier than a word. Placed in a line of poetry, it slows the rhythm and draws attention to itself in a way the original never did. If I keep the meaning, I lose the music; if I keep the music, I lose some of the meaning.

Every translation is built from hundreds of decisions like this one. Should a joke be translated literally, so that readers understand what was said, or replaced with a different joke, so that readers laugh where the original audience laughed? Should an old-fashioned phrase sound old-fashioned in English, or should it sound as natural to modern readers as it once did to the original ones? There is no rule that settles these questions. There is only judgment, and judgment can always be argued with.

For this reason, I have come to think of translation less as copying than as performance. A pianist playing a sonata does not change the notes the composer wrote, yet no two pianists play it the same way, and we do not say that one of them has betrayed the music. We say that each has interpreted it. A translator, too, is an interpreter, faithful not to every word but to what she understands the work to be doing.

This view does not make every translation equally good. A performance can be careless or wrongheaded, and so can a translation. But it does free the translator from an impossible standard and replaces it with a demanding one: not to reproduce the original, but to give it a second life.

choices: the process of matching each word to its exact equivalent.

an impossible task that should not be attempted.
a skill that requires no special training.
5b050000-0003-4000-8000-000000000019.explanation: The author describes translation as performance and the translator as an interpreter making judgments.

Passage IV — Natural Science: This passage is adapted from an article about tardigrades.

Tardigrades, sometimes called water bears, are among the toughest animals known. Most species are less than a millimeter long, with plump bodies and eight stubby legs ending in claws. They live almost everywhere: in ocean sediments, in hot springs, in Antarctic ice, and — most commonly — in the thin film of water that coats mosses and lichens.

That film of water is the key to their reputation. A patch of moss may dry out completely in a single sunny afternoon. Many animals living there would die, but tardigrades respond by entering a state called anhydrobiosis, meaning "life without water." As it dries, a tardigrade pulls in its legs and head and curls into a compact, barrel-shaped form known as a tun. Its metabolism slows to an almost undetectable level. Pill bugs are small land crustaceans. A student studied which conditions pill bugs prefer using a rectangular chamber divided into two equal halves. In each trial, 20 pill bugs were placed in the center of the chamber, and the number of pill bugs in each half was counted after 10 minutes. Each experiment was performed 3 times with new pill bugs.

Experiment 1
One half of the chamber contained dry paper towel; the other contained moist paper towel. Both halves were lit.
Trial: 1 | 2 | 3
Dry half: 4 | 3 | 5
Moist half: 16 | 17 | 15

Experiment 2
Both halves contained moist paper towel. One half was covered to make it dark; the other was lit.
Trial: 1 | 2 | 3
Lit half: 6 | 7 | 5
Dark half: 14 | 13 | 15

Experiment 3
One half was dry and dark; the other half was moist and lit.
Trial: 1 | 2 | 3
Dry and dark half: 9 | 11 | 10
Moist and lit half: 11 | 9 | 10

choices: amount of light in each half of the chamber.
moisture level of each half of the chamber.
number of pill bugs counted in each half.
5b060000-0002-4000-8000-000000000008.explanation: Experiment 1 changed whether each half was dry or moist; the counts were the dependent variable.

notes.3: The counts are what was measured — the dependent variable.

Passage IV

Over the past 20 years, the population of a native fish species in a large lake has declined by about half. During this period, the average summer surface temperature of the lake rose by 2°C, and average summer dissolved oxygen levels in deep water fell slightly. Zebra mussels, an invasive species that filters plankton from the water, were first found in the lake 10 years ago. Since then, plankton levels in the lake have fallen by about 60%. Young fish of the native species feed mainly on plankton. Two scientists discuss the cause of the decline.

Scientist 1
The decline is mainly caused by warming. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water, and the native fish need cool, oxygen-rich deep water in summer. As the lake has warmed, the amount of suitable summer habitat has shrunk, crowding the fish and lowering their survival. The mussels may affect plankton, but the fish population had already begun to decline before the mussels arrived.

Scientist 2
The decline is mainly caused by zebra mussels. By filtering enormous amounts of plankton, the mussels have reduced the food available to young fish, so fewer young fish survive to become adults. Dissolved oxygen levels have fallen only slightly and remain above the level the fish need. Most of the population decline has occurred in the last 10 years, after the mussels became established.
5b060000-0004-4000-8000-000000000022.prompt: Scientist 1 attributes the fish decline mainly to:
choices: a disease spreading among the fish.
warmer water reducing suitable oxygen-rich habitat.
5b060000-0004-4000-8000-000000000022.explanation: Scientist 1 says warming has shrunk cool, oxygen-rich summer habitat.

5b030000-0005-4000-8000-000000000047.passage:
Passage I — The Night Shift
At 3:00 a.m., when most of the town is asleep, the lights in Delgado's Bakery are already __on__. My uncle Marco has run and operated the bakery for a period of twenty years, and last summer I joined him on the night shift.

The first thing I learned was that bread can't be rushed. Dough needs time to rise, and Marco checks it the way a doctor checks a patient, pressing it gently with one finger to see how quickly it springs back. Although the dough is ready, we shape it into loaves, braids, and rolls, working side by side at the long steel table.

Marco rarely talks while he works. At first I found the silence uncomfortable, but after a few nights I began to notice what filled it: the hum of the ovens, the soft thump of dough on the table, and the radio playing quietly in the corner.

By 6:00 a.m., the first customers begin arriving. A nurse coming off her own night shift buys two croissants every morning. A construction crew orders a dozen rolls for their break, Marco knows each of them by name.

When I asked him why he still works nights after all these years, he pauses for a moment before answering. "Because," he said, "were the first people to see the day begin." I didn't fully understand his answer until the last morning of summer, when I carried the final tray of bread to the front window just as the sun raised over the hardware store across the street.

choices: on and the ovens are warming
5b030000-0005-4000-8000-000000000047.explanation: Warming ovens show that the night's work is underway, which the other choices don't convey.

Passage II — Libraries That Grow
In the lobby of some public libraries, next to the newspapers and the community bulletin board, sits an unusual collection: a cabinet __containing__ hundreds of small paper envelopes. Each envelope holds seeds — tomatoes, beans, sunflowers, squash — that anyone with a library card can borrow for free.

These seed libraries work much like book libraries. Patrons take seeds in the spring, grow the plants, and at the end of the season return some of the seeds their plants produced. However, the collection renews itself every year.

Supporters say seed libraries do more than provide free food, many of the seeds are heirloom varieties, plants whose seeds have been saved and passed down for generations. By encouraging gardeners to grow these varieties, seed libraries help preserve plants that otherwise might disappear.

Seed libraries also preserves local knowledge. Because seeds saved in a particular town come from plants that thrived there, each new generation is a little better suited to the area's soil and climate. Gardeners often leave notes in the envelopes, too, offering advice such as "plant after the last frost" or "these need lots of water."

Seeds come in many shapes and sizes. Volunteers sort and label donations, and some gardeners return seeds that are moldy or mislabeled. Still, librarians whom run them say the effort is worth it. As one put it, "Its the only part of our collection that grows."

In the lobby of some public libraries, next to the newspapers and the community bulletin board, sits an unusual collection: a cabinet containing hundreds of small paper envelopes. Each envelope holds seeds — tomatoes, beans, sunflowers, squash — that anyone with a library card can borrow for free.

These seed libraries work much like book __libraries__. Patrons take seeds in the spring, grow the plants, and at the end of the season return some of the seeds their plants produced. However, the collection renews itself every year.

Supporters say seed libraries do more than provide free food, many of the seeds are heirloom varieties, plants whose seeds have been saved and passed down for generations. By encouraging gardeners to grow these varieties, seed libraries help preserve plants that otherwise might disappear.

Seed libraries also preserves local knowledge. Because seeds saved in a particular town come from plants that thrived there, each new generation is a little better suited to the area's soil and climate. Gardeners often leave notes in the envelopes, too, offering advice such as "plant after the last frost" or "these need lots of water."

Seeds come in many shapes and sizes. Volunteers sort and label donations, and some gardeners return seeds that are moldy or mislabeled. Still, librarians whom run them say the effort is worth it. As one put it, "Its the only part of our collection that grows."
5b030000-0006-4000-8000-000000000061.prompt: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
5b030000-0006-4000-8000-000000000061.explanation: "Libraries" is a simple plural here; nothing is possessed.

5b030000-0007-4000-8000-000000000072.passage:
Passage III — Finding North
Long before compasses and satellites, travelers found their way by reading the sky. Last fall, I decided to find out whether I could do the __same?__

On a clear night at a state park, far from the glow of city lights, I lay on a blanket with a star chart and a red flashlight. Red light, I had read, help the eyes adjust to darkness better than white light does. It took nearly twenty minutes before the faint stars appeared, but when they did, the sky seemed to have some with them.

My first goal was to find Polaris, the North Star. Polaris is'nt the brightest star in the sky, as many people assume, but it is useful because it sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole. However, it appears nearly fixed in place while the other stars wheel slowly around it. To find it, I followed the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl, who point toward Polaris like an arrow.

Once I found it, I faced it squarely. North was in front of me, south was at my back, east was to my right, and west was to my left.

Later, I learned that the angle between Polaris and the horizon roughly equals the observer's own personal latitude. Sailors once used this fact to judge how far north they had traveled. Lying in the dark that night, I felt a small connection to the countless, many people who had looked up at the same star and known exactly where they were.

5b030000-0007-4000-8000-000000000072.explanation: The sentence is a statement, so it ends with a period.

5b050000-0005-4000-8000-000000000037.passage:
Passage I — Literary Narrative: This passage is from a short story.

My grandmother learned to swim the summer she turned seventy. She announced it at dinner in June, the way other people announce they are taking up gardening, and then she looked at me.

"You're on the swim team," she said. "You'll teach me."

I was sixteen and had planned to spend the summer doing as little as possible. But there was no arguing with her when she used that tone, so on the first Saturday of July I met her at the community pool. She was already there, sitting on the edge of the shallow end in a borrowed swimsuit, her feet in the water and her hands gripping the tiles.

"I've been here twenty minutes," she said. "I'm getting used to it."

For the first week, we never left the shallow end. I showed her how to put her face in the water and blow bubbles, how to float on her back while I held a hand under her shoulders. She did everything I asked, but carefully, the way she might have handled a dish she suspected was hot. When I let go during the back float, she sank, came up sputtering, and grabbed the side of the pool. I expected her to quit. Instead she wiped her eyes and said, "Again."

It was in the second week that she told me why. When she was a girl, her older brother had nearly drowned in the river behind their farm. Afterward, their mother had forbidden all of the children to go near the water. "I spent sixty years being afraid of something I'd never even tried," she said. "I decided I was finished with that."

By August she could swim a full length of the pool — slowly, her head held high above the water like a cautious turtle, but without stopping. I walked alongside her on the deck the first time she did it. When she reached the far wall, she held on and laughed, and several people in the next lane clapped.

I have won races since then, some of them important ones. None of them felt quite like that.

5b050000-0006-4000-8000-000000000046.passage:
Passage II — Social Science: This passage is adapted from an article about memory.

Ask people to listen to a list of twenty unrelated words and then write down as many as they can remember, and a curious pattern appears. Most people recall the first few words and the last few words far better than the words in the middle. Psychologists call this pattern the serial position effect, and it has been observed in studies of memory for well over a century.

The pattern has two parts. The advantage for early items is called the primacy effect; the advantage for late items is called the recency effect. Researchers believe the two have different causes. Early words, the usual explanation goes, receive more mental rehearsal: when a person hears the first word, it is the only thing to think about, so it can be repeated silently several times. Each new word must share that attention with the words that came before it, so words in the middle get less rehearsal. The last few words, by contrast, are still held in short-term memory when the person begins to write, so they can be recalled almost immediately.

Experiments support this division. When people are asked to count backward for thirty seconds before recalling a list, the recency effect largely disappears — the delay pushes the last words out of short-term memory — while the primacy effect remains. When words are presented very quickly, leaving little time for rehearsal, the primacy effect weakens but the recency effect does not.

The serial position effect has practical consequences. Interviewers may remember the first and last candidates of the day more clearly than those in between. Students cramming a long list of facts may find the middle items slipping away. Some researchers suggest simple remedies: breaking long lists into shorter ones, reviewing the middle items more often, or changing the order of material from one study session to the next.

None of this means that memory works like a recording device with a weak middle. Rather, it shows that what people remember depends not only on what they experience but also on when, and in what order, they experience it.

choices: argue that human memory is unreliable in every situation.
explain a pattern in how people remember lists and what may cause it.
describe the history of psychology as a science.
teach readers how to conduct job interviews.
5b050000-0006-4000-8000-000000000046.explanation: The passage defines the serial position effect, explains its causes and evidence, and notes its consequences.

5b050000-0007-4000-8000-000000000055.passage:
Passage III — Humanities: This passage is adapted from an essay about early portrait photography.

Look through a collection of photographs from the mid-1800s and you will notice that almost no one is smiling. Men and women stare at the camera with closed mouths and level gazes, as if they were sitting for a judge rather than a photographer. It is tempting to conclude that people in the past were simply more serious than we are. The real explanation is more interesting.

Part of the answer is technical. The earliest photographic processes required long exposures, sometimes several minutes, during which the subject had to remain perfectly still. A broad smile is hard to hold for that long; it soon becomes a strained grimace. Photographers' studios even used hidden braces to keep sitters' heads from moving. By the 1850s, however, exposure times had dropped to a matter of seconds, and yet the unsmiling portraits continued for decades. Technology alone cannot explain the pattern.

The rest of the answer lies in tradition. Early photographers and their customers borrowed their ideas about portraits from painting, and painted portraits had long favored calm, composed expressions. In that tradition, a wide grin suggested foolishness or drunkenness, not dignity. A portrait was also a significant purchase, often the only image of a person that a family would ever own. Sitters wanted to be remembered as serious, respectable people, and a solemn expression served that goal.

Over time, both conditions changed. Inexpensive cameras made photography an everyday activity rather than a formal occasion, and people began to photograph one another at picnics, on beaches, and at parties. Advertisements encouraged amateurs to capture happy moments. A photograph no longer had to stand for a person's entire life; it could record a single afternoon. The smile, once out of place, became the expected expression.

Seen this way, those stern Victorian faces are not evidence of gloomier lives. They are a record of what people believed a photograph was for.

5b050000-0007-4000-8000-000000000055.explanation: The author gives technical and cultural reasons and concludes the faces aren't evidence of gloomier lives.

Passage III — Humanities: This passage is adapted from an essay about early portrait photography.

Look through a collection of photographs from the mid-1800s and you will notice that almost no one is smiling. Men and women stare at the camera with closed mouths and level gazes, as if they were sitting for a judge rather than a photographer. It is tempting to conclude that people in the past were simply more serious than we are. The real explanation is more interesting.

Part of the answer is technical. The earliest photographic processes required long exposures, sometimes several minutes, during which the subject had to remain perfectly still. A broad smile is hard to hold for that long; it soon becomes a strained grimace. Photographers' studios even used hidden braces to keep sitters' heads from moving. By the 1850s, however, exposure times had dropped to a matter of seconds, and yet the unsmiling portraits continued for decades. Technology alone cannot explain the pattern.

The rest of the answer lies in tradition. Early photographers and their customers borrowed their ideas about portraits from painting, and painted portraits had long favored calm, composed expressions. In that tradition, a wide grin suggested foolishness or drunkenness, not dignity. A portrait was also a significant purchase, often the only image of a person that a family would ever own. Sitters wanted to be remembered as serious, respectable people, and a solemn expression served that goal.

Over time, both conditions changed. Inexpensive cameras made photography an everyday activity rather than a formal occasion, and people began to photograph one another at picnics, on beaches, and at parties. Advertisements encouraged amateurs to capture happy moments. A photograph no longer had to stand for a person's entire life; it could record a single afternoon. The smile, once out of place, became the expected expression.

Seen this way, those stern Victorian faces are not evidence of gloomier lives. They are a record of what people believed a photograph was for.

Passage IV — Natural Science: This passage is adapted from an article about autumn leaves.

Each autumn, the forests of the northeastern United States turn from green to yellow, orange, and red. The display is so familiar that it is easy to overlook the chemistry behind it, but the change involves several different pigments, each with its own story.

Through spring and summer, leaves are green because they are packed with chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll breaks down in sunlight and must be constantly replaced, so a healthy summer leaf is continually manufacturing it. Leaves also contain yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids, the same compounds that color carrots and egg yolks. During the summer, however, these pigments are hidden by the far more abundant chlorophyll.

As days grow shorter and nights grow cooler in autumn, trees prepare to drop their leaves. A layer of cells forms at the base of each leaf stem, gradually cutting off the flow of water and nutrients. The leaf stops making chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll that remains breaks down. As the green fades, the carotenoids that were present all along become visible, producing yellows and oranges.

Reds and purples have a different origin. They come from pigments called anthocyanins, which many trees, such as some maples, actively produce in autumn. Anthocyanins form from sugars trapped in the leaf, and their production is favored by bright, sunny days followed by cool nights. This is why the same forest may be brilliantly red one year and relatively dull the next: weather during the weeks before the leaves fall strongly affects how much anthocyanin is made.

Why would a tree spend energy making new pigments in leaves it is about to lose? Scientists are still debating the question. One leading hypothesis holds that anthocyanins act as a kind of sunscreen, protecting the leaf's machinery from light damage while the tree withdraws valuable nutrients, such as nitrogen, to store over the winter.

choices: why trees in the Northeast grow taller than trees elsewhere.
the pigments that produce autumn leaf colors and why they appear.
how to identify different species of maple.
5b050000-0008-4000-8000-000000000064.explanation: The passage explains chlorophyll, carotenoids, and anthocyanins and their roles in fall color.

Passage IV

About 66 million years ago, roughly three-quarters of Earth's plant and animal species, including all non-bird dinosaurs, became extinct. Rock layers from this time contain unusually high levels of iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but more common in some asteroids. A crater about 180 kilometers wide in Mexico has been dated to the same time. During the same period, massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India released enormous amounts of lava and gases over hundreds of thousands of years. Two scientists discuss the cause of the extinction.

Scientist 1
The extinction was caused mainly by an asteroid impact. The impact produced the crater in Mexico and threw dust and soot high into the atmosphere, blocking sunlight for months to years. Photosynthesis collapsed, food chains broke down, and many species died out within a geologically short time. The iridium layer, found at sites around the world, marks the debris from this single event. Fossil records show many groups disappearing abruptly at the iridium layer.

Scientist 2
The extinction was caused mainly by volcanic eruptions. Over hundreds of thousands of years, the eruptions released large amounts of carbon dioxide and sulfur gases, changing the climate and making the oceans more acidic. Some species were already declining before the iridium layer was deposited. Volcanic eruptions can also bring iridium from deep within Earth to the surface. An asteroid impact may have added stress, but ecosystems had already been weakened by the long-term effects of volcanism.
5b060000-0009-4000-8000-000000000057.prompt: Scientist 1 attributes the extinction mainly to:
choices: a gradual cooling of the oceans.
5b060000-0009-4000-8000-000000000057.explanation: "The extinction was caused mainly by an asteroid impact."
